questions.a: 2. The product is below 400, so B is 1, 2 or 3, and 4 x B ends in C. B = 1 needs A1 x 4 = 144, so A1 = 36, which does not end in 1. B = 3 needs A3 x 4 = 322, which is not a multiple of 4. B = 2 gives C = 8 and A2 x 4 = 288, so A2 = 72: 72 x 4 = 288.

questions.q:
In AB x 7 = BCA, the product is a 3-digit number that begins with the units digit of AB and ends with its tens digit. (Different letters stand for different digits, and no number begins with 0.)
(a) Explain why B is at most 6, and how the units column links A to B.
(b) Test the possible values of B and find the solution.
questions.a: (a) AB is less than 100, so AB x 7 is less than 700 and its first digit B is at most 6 (and not 0). The product ends in A, so A is the units digit of 7 x B. (b) B = 1: A = 7, but 71 x 7 = 497 begins with 4. B = 2: A = 4, and 42 x 7 = 294 works (C = 9). B = 3: A = 1, but 13 x 7 = 91 has 2 digits. B = 4: A = 8, but 84 x 7 = 588 begins with 5. B = 5: A = 5 = B. B = 6: A = 2, but 26 x 7 = 182 begins with 1. The only solution is 42 x 7 = 294.
s: Part (a): B is at most 6 since the product is below 700; A is the units digit of 7 x B
Part (b): tests B = 1 to 6 and finds 42 x 7 = 294

questions.q:
Rahul turns the true fact 24 x 3 = 72 into the cryptarithm AB x 3 = CA. (Different letters stand for different digits, and no number begins with 0.)
(a) Show that his puzzle has another solution besides 24 x 3 = 72.
(b) Rewrite the puzzle by printing one digit in place of a letter so that 24 x 3 = 72 is the only solution, and justify.
questions.a: (a) 17 x 3 = 51 also fits AB x 3 = CA (A = 1, B = 7, C = 5). (b) Print the 7: AB x 3 = 7A. The product must lie from 70 to 79, so AB is 24, 25 or 26; 24 x 3 = 72 ends in 2 = A, 25 x 3 = 75 ends in 5, not 2, and 26 x 3 = 78 ends in 8, not 2. So 24 x 3 = 72 is the only solution.
s: Part (a): finds 17 x 3 = 51
Part (b): writes a version such as AB x 3 = 7A
Part (b): justifies that only 24 fits

questions.q: A lock opens with a 2-digit code AB that satisfies AB x 9 = BAC. (Each letter is one digit, different letters are different digits, and no number starts with 0.) What is the code?

Tara makes cryptarithms by hiding digits of true multiplications: the same digit gets the same letter, and different digits get different letters. (Different letters stand for different digits, and no number begins with 0.)
From 13 x 7 = 91 she gets AB x 7 = CA. From 12 x 7 = 84 her friend gets AB x 7 = CD.
(a) Explain why, in both puzzles, AB must be 10, 11, 12, 13 or 14.
(b) Show that 13 x 7 = 91 is the only solution of AB x 7 = CA.
(c) Find all the solutions of AB x 7 = CD.
(d) Tara's brother turns 14 x 7 = 98 into a puzzle in the same way, and says this adds a third, different puzzle to their collection. Is he right? Use (c).
questions.a: (a) The product has only 2 digits, and 15 x 7 = 105, so AB is at most 14. (b) 10 x 7 = 70 would need A = 0; 11 repeats a digit; 12 x 7 = 84 would need A = 4; 14 x 7 = 98 would need A = 8. Only 13 x 7 = 91 has A = 1 in both places. (c) 12 x 7 = 84 and 14 x 7 = 98; 10 x 7 = 70 repeats 0, 11 repeats 1 and 13 x 7 = 91 makes D = 1 = A. So there are two solutions. (d) No. 14 x 7 = 98 has four different digits in the pattern 'two-digit x 7 = two-digit', so hiding them gives AB x 7 = CD, the friend's puzzle again; (c) already found 14 x 7 = 98 as one of its two solutions. It is not a new puzzle.
s: Part (a): 15 x 7 = 105, so AB is at most 14
Part (b): only 13 x 7 = 91 fits CA
Part (c): two solutions, 12 x 7 = 84 and 14 x 7 = 98
Part (d): no; 14 x 7 = 98 gives AB x 7 = CD again, whose solutions in (c) include 98

questions.q:
Solve AB + AB + AB + AB = CBB. (Different letters stand for different digits, and no number begins with 0.)
(a) Explain why B must be 0.
(b) Find A and C.
questions.a: (a) The units digit of 4 x B must be B, so 3 x B ends in 0, which happens only for B = 0. (b) A0 x 4 = C00, so 40 x A = 100 x C, that is 2A = 5C. With A not 0, A = 5 and C = 2: 50 + 50 + 50 + 50 = 200.
s: Part (a): 3 x B ends in 0, so B = 0

questions.q: Guna says: 'The cryptarithm AB x B = CAB has exactly one solution, 25 x 5 = 125.' (Usual rules: one digit per letter, a different digit for each letter, no leading 0.) Examine his claim and give your verdict.
questions.a: Guna is only partly right. 25 x 5 = 125 is a solution, but not the only one. B x B must end in B, so B is 0, 1, 5 or 6. B = 0 gives 0 and B = 1 gives a 2-digit product. B = 6: A6 x 6 = CA6 gives 50A + 30 = 100C, which no digits satisfy. B = 5: A5 x 5 = CA5 gives 40A + 20 = 100C, so 2A + 1 = 5C: A = 2, C = 1 (25 x 5 = 125) or A = 7, C = 3 (75 x 5 = 375). So there are two solutions.
s: Narrows B to 0, 1, 5 or 6 from the units digit
Finds the second solution 75 x 5 = 375
Verdict: partly right; his solution is valid but there are two

questions.q: The puzzle AB x 6 = CDB has many solutions. (Each letter is one digit, different letters are different digits, and no number starts with 0.) Four students each send in one answer. Whose answer follows every rule?
questions.a: 28 x 6 = 168 (A = 2, B = 8, C = 1, D = 6, all different). 24 x 6 = 144 makes D = B = 4; 18 x 6 = 108 makes C = A = 1; 12 x 6 = 72 has only 2 digits, so it does not fit CDB.
